title: Research Bite #81: Too High? Teacher Expectations and their (Curvi)linear Associations with Students' School Engagement, Academic Achievement, and School Performance Pressure
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton breaks down a Dutch study by Hornstra and colleagues that asks whether teachers' expectations of pupils can ever be too high. Forty-five teachers predicted how 716 upper primary pupils would do in reading and maths, and the researchers compared those predictions with the pupils' latest results before tracking engagement, achievement and felt pressure across the year. Overestimated pupils made more progress in reading and maths, and those overestimated in maths became more engaged, with no ceiling found for learning. Misjudging pupils in either direction was linked to more pressure, and pupils whose teachers expected too little felt it most. Barton turns the findings into classroom moves: compare your expectations with test data, seek out struggling pupils with achievable challenge, and check who you tend to overestimate. He closes with sensible cautions that the design is correlational, pressure was measured with a single question and the effects were small.
points: High teacher expectations were linked to more progress with no sign of a ceiling, so aiming high remains the right default.
Very low expectations were associated with the most felt pressure, which challenges the assumption that pressure comes only from expecting too much.
Teachers matched pupils' latest results in only about 43% of reading and 50% of maths predictions, so writing down expectations and checking them against data is a worthwhile habit.
Overestimation favoured boys and pupils with more educated parents, so teachers should audit who receives extension work and harder questions.
Ambitious class targets need visible steps and support, and talk should focus on each pupil's own progress rather than comparison with classmates.
quotes: High expectations went hand in hand with more learning, with no sign of a ceiling. Misjudging pupils in either direction was linked to more pressure from schoolwork, and pupils whose teachers expected too little felt it most.

In this study, however, very low expectations looked even more damaging for pressure than very high ones, and lower-attaining pupils felt more pressure overall. The authors suggest that low expectations may tell pupils, without anyone saying it, that they are unlikely to succeed.

Their predictions matched pupils’ most recent results for only about 43% of pupils in reading and 50% in maths. At the start of the year, jot down the level you expect each pupil to reach, then compare your list with their last test results.
When you set ambitious goals, show the steps to reach them, build in support along the way, and talk about each pupil’s progress rather than comparing them with classmates.

Teachers overestimated boys more than girls in reading, and pupils whose parents had more education more than other pupils. Whole classes with more pupils from minority ethnic backgrounds were also overestimated more.

The study is correlational, so overestimation may not have caused the gains; teachers may have noticed qualities the tests missed. Pressure was measured once, with a single question, and the effects were small.

Overall, our findings indicate that high teacher expectations are generally beneficial for students’ school engagement and academic achievement. At the same time, substantial overestimation may increase the risk of heightened performance pressure.
